You should try the following : check your connection, disable ad-blocker, clear your browser cache, try in private mode, try from another browser/computer/connection. 0 New Frontiers In New Frontiers, a standalone game in the Race for the Galaxy family, players build galactic empires by selecting, in turn, an action that everyone may do, with only the selecting player gaining that action's bonus. The developments to be used are determined during setup, allowing players to make strategic plans based on them before play begins. One group of eight developments is always in play. The game includes a suggested set of sixteen additional developments for your first game; in later games, players randomly select which side of eight double-sided "small" developments and eight double-sided "large" 9-cost developments to use during setup. Many worlds that players can acquire have special powers, with these worlds being drawn from a bag during the Explore phase. Unlike in Race, in New Frontiers worlds need colonists to be settled, in addition to either payments or conquest. Some worlds are "windfall" worlds and receive a good upon being settled. Others are production worlds and receive goods when the Produce action is selected. Goods can be traded for credits or consumed for victory points. Play continues until one or more of four game ending conditions is reached. After all actions for that round have been done, the player with the most victory points from settled worlds, developments, 9-cost development bonuses, and VP chips earned from consuming goods wins. Number of players: 2 - 5 Game duration: 32 mn Complexity: 3 / 5 Play New Frontiers and 1414 other games online. No download necessary - play directly from your web browser. With your friends and thousands of players from the whole world. Free. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Play 2 Actions 2.1 Retreat into Isolation 2.2 Develop 2.3 Explore 2.4 Settle 2.5 Produce 2.6 Trade/Consume 2.7 Send Diplomatic Envoys 3 Game End 4 Winning Play Players take turns to select actions. Each player, in order on the priority track, does that action, with the selecting player receiving its bonus. As a player is taking their turn, their disk shifts half way between spaces on the priority track. Following players select action tiles that have not already been selected. In 2-player games, each player selects two actions and each action is done only once by each player. Once everyone has selected, if Produce was not selected, 1 credit is added to its tile and a new round begins. Some action tiles have no associated action; they only grant a bonus to the selecting player. Priority order does not change from round to round, unless an action or goal alters it. Actions Retreat into Isolation Action: None Bonus: Gain 2 credits Develop Action: buy 1 development. Bonus: −1 cost. Most developments provide a power which modifies the rules. Each development built will score victory points at game end equal to the number in its hexagon. The “?” on the 9-cost developments indicates a variable number of victory points that will be scored at game end, as detailed on that tile. Explore Action: pick 1 world from 7 Bonus: pick a second world (after everyone has picked a world). Explored worlds have not been settled yet. They go on the right of your mat. An explored world's powers, VPs are inactive until that world is settled. You cannot have more than 9 colonies - explored or settled. Any excess are discarded. Settle Bonus: gain 1 colonist. Action: either gain 2 colonists or settle 1 world. The selecting player gains one colonist. Then each player either gains two colonists or settles one explored world, converting it into a colony. The selecting player gains their bonus colonist first and may use that colonist to immediately settle a world. To settle an explored world, a player must have both its listed number of colonists — one or two — and either sufficient credits or military strength to place it, depending on the world’s type: non-military or military. A non-military world has a black circle and a solid black number, its cost, which must be paid in credits to settle that world. A military world has a red circle and an outlined red number, its defense, which the empire’s total Military must equal or exceed to settle (conquer) that world. [Rating: 1/10] Terrible attempt at reworking Race for the Galaxy back into the same system of Puerto Rico that was the inspiration for RftG, Puerto Rico gains nothing from the backported changes of Race while RftG gains nothing by expanding into a big boardgame. Truly just a game that gives no reason for it to exist beyond $$$.

[Rating: 1/10] I don't like Race for the Galaxy. I can tolerate Puerto Rico. Both of those games are still better than this one. Setup took too long. Teach took too long.

[Rating: 3/10] When I first heard about Roll for the Galaxy I sincerely wondered why that game should exist. Upon playing it, my expectations were overturned by a wonderfully deep system that I ultimately found mo engaging than the original.   New Frontiers I went into with a very open mind, largely due to the aforementioned rejection, but came away feeling my original Roll criticism was well placed here.   It's big, clunky, expensive, and ultimately offers little the other titles do not. New Frontiers gives more long term strategic options to new players, but that distinction feels smaller than I expected a

[Rating: 3/10] Completely uneccessary. Adds nothing to the genre. Stick with RftG and Puerto Rico.

[Rating: 3/10] The cool theme is just slapped on, I did not get the sci-fi feal at all.  The planets is not balanced at all, some are just better then others. These planets is drawn from a bag and even if you draw 7 it can really destroy your game.  Players will fight over 3-4 colors of planets, If you are lucky you will target a color from the beginning that no one else have taken. If not you will have a hard time, specally if its military.  Military do also not have anything to do with war, its just a color, nothing more.

[Rating: 3/10] Like Race for the Galaxy (that I like) plus Puerto Rico (that I like too). All in all a good game.

[Rating: 3/10] Nearly as awful as the game that inspired it. The fact that this was a warmed-over version of Puerto Rico is especially evident here with the return of colonists…  At least there’s a tableau you can pull some basic tech from, which is a slight improvement over “draw what you get & hope for some crap that have synergies” of the original RFtG.

[Rating: 3/10] Played one game with my SO. We found the game so boring that we stopped halfway. Its pretty the same thing all game, with baby step progress, but youre basically just owning new planets and there are no BIG plays going on. Good gateway game maybe? Pretty straightforward, you dont need to think that much. I'm amazed that game is 7.5. I would not recommend game to my friends. My biggest criticism is the price tag. That game goes for around 80$, but dont deliver much for that price and yet, I bought it half price and I wasnt even satisfied for what I payed for it. Biggest point is maybe the produ

[Rating: 4/10] I purchased this thinking it would combine my favorite things about RftG and Puerto Rico. Turns out, it does the opposite. Settlement strategies are MORE luck-dependent than they are in RftG, and games are 2-3x as long. The lack of perfect information and a fixed turn order makes turn sequencing more prone to chaos than Puerto Rico.  I don't see a time when I would choose this over either of its predecessors.

[Rating: 4/10] Update: Well three years and a BGA implementation later and the game is really starting to show its flaws.  First, Retreat Into Isolation is such a good action, it's is often the thing you should do. It's even common to open with it on Round 1 as Player 1. As the top player on BGA rightly identified: RII is the action by which you must judge all of your decision making. Is this thing I'm about to do better than getting $2? [Rating: 4/10] It's okay. The biggest issue is related to exploring. If you have anyone in your group prone to AP, you have 2-3 others waiting for that person to look at 7 tiles and decide which one is best for them. The game has a lot of downtime, tiny text and a lot of things to look at.   In terms of engine building, everything that Gizmos gets right, this game misses the mark. Namely clarity of function, simplicity of options and streamlined turns.   If they address the explore downtime (3-5 minutes!), it would improve the game significantly.

[Rating: 4/10] Same fault as Race for the Galaxy. Planets are super random and a luck factor is way to big. There are a display with developments, why not do the same thing with the planets and suddenly you have a good game.

[Rating: 4/10] did not like this very much. I like both Race for the Galaxy and Puerto Rico better. I prefer the cards being what you build and being money from race to the separate money in this. And I prefer being able to build buildings and then later fix that they get manned and start working to needing a dude before I can get a planet.

[Rating: 4/10] Race for the Galaxy, the boardgame. Not bad, but why?  It is not better than the original, but longer. It is different from, but definitely not better than Puerto Rico.
